why: Why does the air above a city stay warm long after sunset?
we: used to refer to the speaker and one or more other people
We forget most of what we just learned within a day.
forget: Try not to forget your umbrella; it might rain later.
what: used to ask for information about something
The reason lies in what cities are actually made of.
just: I just finished reading the report you sent this morning.
learned: gained knowledge or skill through study or experience
She learned to cook traditional dishes from her grandmother.
most: the majority of; the greatest amount or number of
Most of the guests had already left by the time the rain started.
of: used to show belonging, origin, or a relationship between two things
The cover of the book was torn at the corner.
lesson: a period of teaching, or something learned from experience
The teacher planned an interactive lesson about the water cycle.
disappears: stops being visible or ceases to exist
The morning dew usually disappears once the sun rises higher.
within: inside; before a period of time has passed
Most of a lesson disappears within a single day.
day: a period of twenty-four hours, or the time when it is light
She spent the whole day preparing for the interview.
that: used to identify a specific thing, person, or clause already mentioned
The book that you gave me last year is still on my shelf.
is: present tense (he/she/it) of the verb be
The library is open until nine o'clock every evening.
normal: usual, typical, or expected; not unusual
It is normal to feel nervous before a big exam.
and: used to connect words, phrases, or clauses
We packed sandwiches, fruit, and water for the long hike.
it: used to refer to a thing, animal, or situation already mentioned
She lost her phone and later found it under the sofa.
can: used to express ability or possibility
Anyone with an internet connection can join the online course.
be: to exist, or to have a particular state or quality
It can be difficult to stay calm during an emergency.
worked: That is normal, and it can be worked around with a little planning.
around: The children ran around the playground chasing each other happily.
half: one of two equal parts of something
She gave half of the sandwich to her brother.
an: used before a word starting with a vowel sound to mean 'one'
She ordered an apple juice and a sandwich for lunch.
hour: It takes about an hour to drive to the city centre.
after: following in time or place; later than
The shop stays open late after the holiday season begins.
ends: comes to a finish or stop
Half an hour after a lesson ends, much of it is already forgotten.
much: to a great extent or degree
The new design does not cost much more than the old one.
was: past tense of 'be', used for the first/third person singular
Half an hour after a lesson ends, much of what was said is already gone.
said: past tense of say; spoke or expressed something in words
She said the meeting would start at nine o'clock.
in: expressing location inside or within something
The keys are in the top drawer of the desk.
already: before now or before a particular time
By the time we arrived, the meeting had already started.
gone: departed, disappeared, or no longer present
By the time we arrived, the bus was already gone.
this: used to refer to a specific thing nearby or just mentioned
This is the best coffee I have had in years.
not: used to make a statement, verb, or phrase negative
The results are not as clear as we had hoped.
sign: something that indicates the presence or existence of a fact or quality
Dark clouds are often a sign that rain is coming soon.
poor: not good in quality, ability, or amount; weak
The bridge was closed after inspectors found its poor condition dangerous.
memory: the ability to store and recall information
His memory for names and faces has always been impressive.
how: She explained how the machine works in simple terms.
normally: in the usual or expected way; under ordinary conditions
He normally leaves for work before seven in the morning.
behaves: acts or functions in a particular way
The material behaves like rubber when it is heated.
understanding: the ability to grasp the meaning of something; sympathetic awareness
Understanding the pattern is the first step towards working around it.
the: used before a noun to refer to a specific or already-known thing
The cat sat quietly on the windowsill all afternoon.
pattern: a regular, repeated way in which something happens or is arranged
Analysts noticed a clear pattern in the company's sales figures.
first: coming before all others in order or time
She was the first person to arrive at the meeting.
step: one action in a series, or a single movement of the foot
Booking the flight was the first step in planning the trip.
towards: in the direction of; moving closer to
Understanding the pattern is the first step towards working around it.
working: Understanding the pattern is the first step towards working around it.
researchers: people who carry out careful study
Researchers have tracked the glacier's retreat for thirty years.
have: used with a past participle to form perfect tenses
They have finished the report ahead of schedule.
described: said what someone or something is like
Witnesses described the car as dark blue with tinted windows.
fall: a decrease in amount, level, or value
The report records a steady fall in river fish populations.
since: from a particular time in the past until now, or because
He has lived in this city since he graduated from university.
nineteenth: coming after the eighteenth in order; 19th
The museum is housed in a nineteenth-century warehouse.
century: a period of one hundred years
The tradition has been passed down for more than a century.
loss: the fact of no longer having something
The company reported a small loss in its first year.
fastest: moving or acting most quickly; superlative of fast
Cheetahs are the fastest land animals on Earth.
at: used to show a specific place, time or point
We agreed to meet at the station at six o'clock.
start: the beginning or first part of something
The meeting got off to a slow start.
steep: rising or falling sharply; very sudden and large
House prices took a steep drop after the crisis began.
drop: There was a sudden drop in temperature after the storm passed.
then: at that time, or next in a sequence of events
We finished dinner, and then we watched a film together.
slower: moving or happening at a reduced speed, compared with something else
The old computer is much slower than the new one.
decline: a gradual decrease in quality, size, or strength
The company's profits have shown a steady decline over the past two years.
over: during the whole of a period of time; more than
Prices have risen steadily over the past five years.
following: coming next in time or order
They planned to travel again the following spring.
week: The loss is fastest at the start, then slows over the following week.
survives: continues to live or exist after a difficulty
The old tradition still survives in a few remote mountain villages.
month: one of the twelve periods that a year is divided into
She started a new job at the beginning of the month.
only: and no one or nothing more besides; just
Only a handful of tickets remained by the time we arrived.
small: not large in size, amount, or degree
They live in a small apartment near the city center.
part: a piece or portion of a whole
Only a small part of the report dealt with financial risks.
once: immediately, without delay (used in the phrase 'at once')
The fire alarm made everyone leave the building at once.
felt: sensed, perceived, or seemed to be; past tense of feel
She felt a sudden chill as the wind picked up.
perfectly: in a perfect manner; completely or entirely
She remembered the song perfectly even though she had not sung it in years.
clear: easy to understand, see, or perceive; free from confusion
The instructions were clear enough for a beginner to follow.
reason: a cause or explanation for something
Nobody knew the real reason for his sudden resignation.
brain: the organ inside the head that controls thought and body function
Reading regularly keeps the brain active and engaged.
treats: present tense of treat, used with he/she/it
The reason is that the brain treats most new information as temporary.
new: not existing before; recently made, discovered or experienced
They moved into a new apartment near the city centre.
information: facts or details known or given about someone or something
The website provides useful information about local bus routes.
as: used to compare, or to mean 'while' or 'because'
As the sun set, the temperature dropped quickly.
temporary: lasting for only a limited time, not permanent
They found a temporary place to stay while their house was repaired.
fact: a thing that is known to be true
It is a fact that the Earth orbits the Sun.
heard: perceived sound with the ears; past tense of hear
She heard footsteps approaching from behind the door.
looks: appears to be, has a certain appearance
The sky looks heavy with rain this afternoon.
from: indicating the point where something starts or originates
The letter came from a friend living overseas.
inside: the inner part or area of something
The inside of the cave was cool and damp.
exactly: in a way that is precise or correct in every detail
A fact heard once looks exactly like one that will never be needed.
like: similar to, or in the same way as
Her handwriting looks a lot like her mother's.
will: used to express the future tense
A fact heard once looks, from the inside, like a fact that will never be needed again.
never: at no time; not on any occasion
She had never travelled outside her home country before that trip.
needed: The volunteers brought all the supplies needed for the rescue.
again: She read the letter again before deciding what to write back.
unless: except if; on the condition that something does not happen
Unless something marks it as worth keeping, it is allowed to fade.
something: She said something that made everyone in the room laugh.
marks: shows or indicates something, or makes a visible sign on it
A small star marks the correct answer on the page.
worth: having a value or deserving of something
Unless something marks it as worth keeping, it is allowed to fade.
keeping: continuing to have, hold, or maintain something
Keeping old letters can help families remember their history.
allowed: given permission to happen or be done
được để cho, bị bỏ mặc
Visitors are not allowed to touch the ancient manuscripts in the archive.
to: expressing direction, purpose, or a recipient
The sun has set, the traffic has thinned, and yet the air refuses to cool.
fade: to gradually become less bright, strong, or clear
The old photograph had begun to fade after so many years.
two: Two things mark it as worth keeping.
things: plural of thing; objects, ideas, or matters
She packed her things and left the apartment quietly.
mark: to make a visible sign on something; to indicate
Volunteers used flags to mark the edge of the trail.
difficulty: the state of being hard to do or understand
She had no difficulty finishing the race in record time.
costs: requires the payment of a specified amount of money
A round trip by taxi costs more than the entire bus fare for a week.
effort: physical or mental energy used to do something
Learning a new language takes years of steady effort.
recall: to remember something from the past
She could not recall where she had left her umbrella.
stored: Old family photos were stored safely in a metal box.
more: to a greater degree or extent
Careful listeners remember song lyrics more clearly than plain speech.
firmly: in a solid, steady, or determined way
She firmly believes that hard work leads to success.
than: used to introduce the second part of a comparison
This year's harvest was larger than last year's.
simply: in an easy or straightforward way; just, merely
She simply smiled and walked away without saying a word.
reread: I had to reread the paragraph three times to understand it.
second: coming after the first in order
The second attempt succeeded where the first had failed.
spacing: the amount of space left between things
The teacher asked students to check the spacing between paragraphs.
meeting: the act of coming together with someone or something again
Meeting new colleagues can feel awkward at first.
same: They wore the same colour shirts to the reunion.
gap: a difference or space between two things
The gap between rich and poor neighbourhoods keeps growing.
forces: makes someone do something against their will
A tight deadline often forces people to make quick decisions.
rebuild: to build something again after it has been damaged or destroyed
It took years to rebuild the town after the devastating earthquake.
each: every one of two or more things, considered separately
Each student received a copy of the new textbook.
rebuilding: the act of building something again after damage or destruction
The rebuilding of the ancient temple took nearly two decades to finish.
leaves: goes away from a place, or allows something to remain (he/she/it)
The train leaves the station every hour on the hour.
stronger: having more physical or mental power (comparative of strong)
Regular exercise made her noticeably stronger over the year.
trace: a small mark or sign left by something that existed
Meeting the same fact again after a gap forces the brain to rebuild it, leaving a stronger trace.
explains: makes something clear by describing it in detail
This explains why rereading notes feels productive but works so poorly.
rereading: the act of reading something again
Rereading old letters brought back many memories.
notes: short written records made to help someone remember something
She reviewed her notes carefully before the final exam.
feels: The fabric feels soft and warm against the skin.
productive: producing good or useful results efficiently
Employees tend to be more productive after a short break.
works: This explains why rereading notes feels productive and works so poorly.
so: used to show the result or consequence of something
It started raining, so we decided to stay indoors.
poorly: in a bad or unsatisfactory way
The meeting was organized poorly, and half the guests never arrived.
page: one side of a sheet of paper in a book or document
She turned the page slowly, savouring the final chapter.
familiar: The song sounded familiar, though she couldn't remember its name.
recognition: acknowledgement of someone's achievement or existence
The scientist finally received recognition for her groundbreaking discovery.
comes: moves toward or arrives at a place; originates from
Fresh bread comes out of the oven every morning at six.
easily: without difficulty; in an easy manner
The instructions were clear, so we assembled the shelf easily.
easy: The test was easy enough that most students finished early.
feeling: an emotional state or physical sensation
A warm feeling of relief spread through the room.
mistaken: wrongly identified or thought to be something else
The twins are often mistaken for each other by strangers.
for: intended to belong to, or be given to, someone or something
She bought a small gift for her best friend.
knowledge: information, understanding, or skill gained through experience
Her knowledge of local plants proved useful during the hike.
closing: shutting, or coming to an end
Closing the shop early gave staff time to rest before the holiday.
book: a written or printed work with pages bound together
She borrowed a book about ancient history from the library.
trying: present participle of try; making an attempt to do something
Closing the book and trying to write the same content from memory feels far worse but works far better.
write: to produce text using a pen, keyboard or similar tool
Trying to write the same content from memory feels far worse than rereading it.
content: the ideas or information contained in something, such as a book
The website's content is updated with fresh articles every morning.
far: to a great extent; at or to a great distance
This plan works far better than the last one did.
worse: Trying to write the same content from memory feels far worse — and works far better.
better: of higher quality or more suitable than something else
The second recipe turned out much better than the first attempt.
method: a particular way of doing something
Teachers are experimenting with a new method for teaching fractions.
also: The recipe also works well with chicken instead of beef.
while: It makes the city liveable while the wider problem is dealt with separately.
you: used to refer to the person being spoken to
The method also feels worse while you are doing it.
are: present tense form of 'to be' used with you, we, they
They are planning to visit their grandparents next weekend.
doing: What are you doing this weekend?
which: used to ask about or refer to a specific choice
It is one of the clearest ways in which a city changes its weather.
few: a small number of; not many
Only a few students finished the exam before the bell rang.
people: human beings in general, considered as a group of individuals
Many people prefer walking to work during the warm summer months.
stay: to continue to be in a place or condition
She decided to stay with the exercise plan for a full year.
with: Neighbourhoods with few trees heat up fastest, and these are often the poorest districts.
smooth: even and free from bumps, lumps, or roughness
The dancer's movements were smooth and effortless.
produces: The volcano regularly produces small clouds of ash and steam.
pleasant: We had a pleasant afternoon walking along the beach.
sense: a feeling or awareness of something
A sense of relief washed over her when the results arrived.
familiarity: knowledge or experience gained from repeated exposure
Years of practice gave her a deep familiarity with the piano.
testing: the process of checking or examining something
Testing of the new software will continue for another month.
yourself: used to refer back to the person being spoken to
chính bạn, tự bản thân bạn
Testing yourself is slow, and every gap you find feels like a small failure.
slow: The traffic was slow because of the heavy rain.
every: used to refer to each member of a group without exception
Somebody must repaint the roof every few years.
find: I finally found my keys under the sofa.
failure: a lack of success, or something that does not work
The project ended in failure after funding was cut.
studies: pieces of research carried out to examine a subject in detail
Several studies confirm the benefits of regular exercise.
comparing: examining two or more things to note similarities or differences
Comparing the two recipes shows how much sugar the newer one removes.
learners: The course was designed for beginner learners with no prior experience.
consistently: in a way that stays the same over time
The team has consistently finished among the top three this season.
prefer: like one thing better than another
Most students prefer online lectures they can watch at their own pace.
teaches: gives someone knowledge or a skill
She teaches piano to children on weekend afternoons.
them: used to refer to people or things already mentioned, as the object
I called them yesterday but nobody answered the phone.
less: He eats less meat now than he used to.
none: not any of a group of people or things
None of the students had heard of the composer before.
makes: A short walk after dinner makes falling asleep much easier.
learning: the process of gaining knowledge or skill
Online learning has become common since the pandemic.
effortless: The dancer made the difficult routine look effortless.
changes: plural of change; alterations or differences from before
The new law brought major changes to how taxes are collected.
where: It changes where the effort goes, away from the comfortable hours of reading.
goes: moves or travels from one place to another
He goes to the gym every morning before work.
away: to or at a distance from a place or person
The children ran away when they saw the dog.
comfortable: The new chairs in the office are much more comfortable.
hours: The meeting lasted several hours longer than expected.
spent: past tense of spend: used time or money on something
He spent two hours fixing the broken fence yesterday.
looking: He spent the afternoon looking for his missing keys.
pages: sides of paper sheets in a book or document
He flipped through the pages looking for the missing diagram.
uncomfortable: causing or feeling physical or mental unease
It changes where the effort goes, towards the uncomfortable minutes spent trying to remember.
minutes: units of time equal to sixty seconds
The bus arrived only a few minutes late.
remember: to bring a fact or memory back to mind
I can never remember where I left my umbrella.
those: used to refer to people or things further away or already mentioned
Those houses on the hill were built a century ago.
